issues.legal_issue: A delegated authority to regulate mineral concessions may include a prohibition on private leases for a particular mineral when the prohibition serves conservation and prudent exploitation.
material_facts: Black granite was classified as a minor mineral, and the State had authority to make rules regulating concessions for minor minerals.
The rule barred leases to private persons for quarrying black granite but allowed the State or a wholly State-owned corporation to quarry it.
The State gave reasons concerning unsystematic mining, mineral wastage, inadequate worker safety, and the failure of many lessees to establish effective processing industries.
issues.conclusion: The prohibition was within the delegated rule-making power and was a bona fide measure for conservation and prudent exploitation, not a misuse of that power to advance the State’s self-interest.
issues.legal_principle: The purpose of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, including section 15 read with sections 4A, 17 and 18, is the conservation and prudent, discriminating exploitation of minerals for the community’s benefit. In context, “regulation” can include prohibition; its meaning depends on the statute’s purpose and the subject regulated. The Court relied on Municipal Corporation of the City of Toronto v. Virgo, Attorney General for Ontario v. Attorney General for the Dominion, State of Uttar Pradesh v. Hindustan Aluminium Corporation, G. K. Krishnan v. State of Tamil Nadu, and Commonwealth of Australia v. Bank of New South Wales.

predicates.mineral_concession_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule governing concessions to extract a mineral.
predicates.state_authorized_to_regulate_minor_miner: The State had authority to regulate concessions for the category of mineral involved.
predicates.private_extraction_banned_for_conservati: The rule barred private extraction of the mineral for reasons directed to conserving it or ensuring its prudent exploitation.
predicates.public_extraction_remained_available: The rule allowed the State or a State-owned entity to extract the mineral.

issues.definition: When a challenge concerns a mineral-concession rule, the State has authority over the relevant concessions, private extraction is barred for conservation, and public extraction remains available, the rule may prohibit private extraction.

issues.legal_issue: A subordinate rule may reserve extraction of a particular mineral to public entities without requiring separate plenary legislation merely because it shifts extraction from the private to the public sector.
material_facts: The rule ended the grant of new black-granite quarry leases to private persons and permitted quarrying by the State or a wholly State-owned corporation.
The rule concerned one particular mineral and was justified by the stated aim of conserving it and improving its exploitation.
The State had been delegated authority to regulate minor-mineral concessions.
issues.conclusion: The rule did not require separate plenary legislation merely because it reserved quarrying of black granite to public entities; the change did not itself amount to a change in the policy of the governing law.
issues.legal_principle: A transition from private-sector to public-sector activity does not invariably require express legislative sanction; the answer depends on the subject and the governing statute. A restriction on private activity concerning a particular mineral, made within the delegated authority and to advance conservation, may be consistent with the existing policy. The Court relied on H. C. Narayanappa v. State of Mysore, Rai Sahib Ram Jawaya Kapur v. State of Punjab, and the constitutional provisions concerning State trade and legislative authority, including Articles 19(6) and 298 and Entry 21 of List III.

predicates.mineral_concession_rule_challenge: The proceeding challenges a rule governing concessions to extract a mineral.
predicates.state_authorized_to_regulate_minor_miner: The State had authority to regulate concessions for the category of mineral involved.
predicates.restriction_limited_to_particular_minera: The restriction concerned a particular mineral rather than imposing a general ban on private mining of all minerals in the category.
predicates.public_exploitation_selected_for_conserv: Public extraction was selected as the preferred means of conserving or prudently exploiting that mineral.

issues.definition: Where a challenged rule is within the State’s regulatory authority and reserves a particular mineral for public extraction to conserve it, that reservation alone does not require separate plenary legislation.

issues.legal_issue: A mineral-concession rule made under parliamentary authority for regulation and development does not violate the constitutional guarantee of free trade merely because it restricts private extraction.
material_facts: The challenged rule was made under authority delegated by a parliamentary enactment expressly directed to regulating mines and developing minerals in the public interest.
The rule restricted private leases for quarrying black granite, while providing for extraction by the State or a State-owned corporation.
The rule was notified as a statutory rule pursuant to the delegated authority.
issues.conclusion: The Act and rules properly made under it were outside the restrictions prohibited by Article 301, and the public-interest authority in Article 302 also answered the challenge based on Article 301; the asserted constitutional challenge failed.
issues.legal_principle: Article 301 addresses restrictions that directly and immediately impede the free flow or movement of trade; regulatory measures that facilitate or regulate trade are outside its scope. Article 302 permits Parliament to impose restrictions in the public interest. A statutory rule made under delegated authority is to be treated as law for this purpose. The Court relied on Atiabari Tea Co. v. State of Assam, The Automobile Transport (Rajasthan) Ltd. v. State of Rajasthan, and State of U.P. v. Babu Ram Upadhya.

predicates.constitutional_trade_restriction_challen: The proceeding challenges a restriction on mineral activity as inconsistent with constitutional freedom of trade.
predicates.rule_made_under_parliamentary_regulatory: The rule was made under authority conferred by a parliamentary enactment directed to regulating the relevant economic activity.
predicates.rule_is_regulatory_measure: The rule forms part of a regulatory scheme for the activity rather than being an unrelated impediment to trade.
predicates.rule_properly_made: The rule was made within the authority delegated to the rule-maker.

issues.definition: When a properly made rule under parliamentary regulatory authority is challenged as a trade restriction and forms part of the regulatory scheme, it does not violate the constitutional free-trade guarantee.

issues.legal_issue: A rule barring new private leases for a mineral also applies when the authority considers applications to renew existing leases.
material_facts: The governing rules required a renewal applicant to satisfy the authority that renewal served mineral development and that the lease amount was reasonable.
Applications to renew black-granite quarry leases were pending when the rule barring private leases came into force.
The applicants contended that the renewal criteria were separate from the criteria for granting a lease in the first instance.
issues.conclusion: The prohibition applied to renewal applications because renewal is, in substance, a grant for a fresh period and the applicable grant criteria must be applied, suitably adapted, when renewal is considered.
issues.legal_principle: A renewal is not automatic and must satisfy the renewal conditions as well as the criteria applicable to an initial grant, adapted as necessary. Otherwise, a later restriction adopted to conserve a mineral could be defeated by renewals. The Court applied the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, including the renewal rule and the rule governing black-granite leases.

predicates.renewal_application_for_mineral_lease: An applicant sought renewal of a lease to extract a mineral.
predicates.renewal_not_automatic: The governing rules made renewal conditional on the authority’s assessment rather than an entitlement upon request.
predicates.current_rule_bars_private_grants: A rule in force when the renewal application was considered barred the relevant private grants.

issues.definition: If renewal is conditional and the current rule bars the relevant private grants, that bar applies when a mineral-lease renewal is considered.

issues.legal_issue: A pending application for a mineral lease or renewal is governed by the rules in force when the application is decided, even if it was filed before a later rule came into force.
material_facts: Some applications for new leases or renewals were filed before the rule barring private black-granite leases came into force.
The applications remained pending and were decided after that rule came into force.
The applicants argued that delay in deciding their applications entitled them to have them considered under the earlier rules.
The applicants had no vested right to obtain a lease or renewal.
issues.conclusion: The applications had to be decided under the rules in force on the date of disposal; the applicants’ right to a timely decision did not give them a vested right to have the earlier rules applied.
issues.legal_principle: No applicant has a vested right to the grant or renewal of a lease, or to have an application decided under the rules in force when it was filed. An application must be decided under the rules in force when it is disposed of, although it should be dealt with within a reasonable time.

predicates.pending_mineral_lease_application: An application for a new mineral lease or renewal remained undecided.
predicates.later_rule_in_force_before_decision: A new rule relevant to the application came into force before the authority decided it.
predicates.no_vested_right_to_lease: The applicant had no vested right to receive the lease or renewal.

issues.definition: If a mineral-lease application remains pending until a relevant later rule comes into force and the applicant has no vested right to a lease, the rules in force at decision govern.

issues.legal_issue: A rule restricting leases for a mineral on government land does not bar a private owner from seeking permission to extract that mineral from land in which the mineral rights belong to the owner.
material_facts: Some applicants sought permission to quarry black granite on private lands where the mineral rights belonged to them.
The challenged rule concerned leases for quarrying black granite and appeared among rules governing government lands and minerals belonging to the government.
The private owners were not seeking a lease from the government.
issues.conclusion: The rule did not apply to those private lands or impose a general ban on quarrying; the applications had to be dealt with under the rules applicable to privately owned mineral rights.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of a rule is determined by its language and context. A rule barring the grant of leases does not apply where the mineral rights belong to the applicant and no government lease is sought. The Court applied the structure and language of the Tamil Nadu Minor Mineral Concession Rules, distinguishing rules for government lands from those for privately owned mineral rights.

predicates.private_land_mineral_permission_applicat: The proceeding concerns an application for permission to extract a mineral from privately owned land.
predicates.mineral_rights_belong_to_applicant: The applicant owns the mineral rights in the land.
predicates.no_government_lease_sought: The applicant seeks no lease of the mineral rights from the government.

issues.definition: When an applicant seeks permission to extract a mineral from private land, owns the mineral rights, and seeks no government lease, a bar on government leases does not apply.
